topics.name: Life and importance of the Prophet (pbuh)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of the first revelation to the Prophet (pbuh) and what happened immediately afterwards.
parts.answer: At about the age of 40 (610 CE) the Prophet (pbuh) was meditating in the cave of Hira when the angel Jibril came and told him to read; he said he could not read; the angel pressed him three times and then revealed the first verses of Sura 96 (Iqra); he returned home shaken and asked Khadija to cover him; she comforted him, reminding him of his good character, and took him to her cousin Waraqa bin Naufal, who said this was the same angel who had come to Moses and warned that his people would drive him out.
parts.working: Indicative content: Age about 40 / month of Ramadan; retreat in the cave of Hira on Mount Nur; Jibril appeared and commanded 'Read'; the Prophet (pbuh) replied that he could not read; the angel embraced / squeezed him three times; the first verses of Sura 96.1–5 were revealed; he returned trembling and asked to be wrapped up; Khadija reassured him (he is kind to relatives, helps the weak, honours guests); visit to Waraqa bin Naufal; Waraqa confirmed it was the angel who came to Moses and predicted opposition. parts.answer: Spouses should support each other in hard times, listen calmly, encourage each other's good qualities and seek wise advice together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the persecution suffered by early Muslims in Makka. Refer to named individuals.
parts.answer: Bilal was tortured by his master Umayya bin Khalaf, laid on hot sand with a rock on his chest, yet kept saying God is One, until Abu Bakr bought and freed him; Yasir and his wife Sumayya were tortured and Sumayya was killed by Abu Jahl, the first martyr of Islam; their son 'Ammar was also tortured; Khabbab bin al-Aratt was made to lie on burning coals; the Prophet (pbuh) himself was insulted, had filth thrown on him while praying and thorns placed in his path.
parts.working: Indicative content: Bilal — tortured by Umayya bin Khalaf on hot sand with a stone on his chest; repeated 'Ahad, Ahad'; freed by Abu Bakr; Sumayya — killed by Abu Jahl, the first martyr; Yasir also died under torture; 'Ammar tortured; Khabbab — burned on coals; slaves and poor Muslims suffered most; the Prophet (pbuh) was mocked and had dirt / entrails thrown on him; Abu Lahab's wife put thorns in his path. parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of the Night Journey and Ascension (al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj).
parts.answer: One night in Makka, before the Hijra, the angel Jibril took the Prophet (pbuh) from the Sacred Mosque in Makka to al-Aqsa in Jerusalem on al-Buraq; there he led the earlier prophets in prayer; he then ascended through the heavens, meeting prophets such as Adam, Jesus, Moses and Abraham, and reached the Lote Tree of the Furthest Boundary; the five daily prayers were made obligatory (first fifty, reduced to five); in the morning the Quraysh mocked the account, but Abu Bakr believed it at once and was called al-Siddiq.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Prophet (pbuh) began to preach Islam openly in Makka.
parts.answer: After about three years of private preaching, God commanded him to warn his nearest relatives; he invited the Banu Hashim to a meal and called them to Islam, and only 'Ali responded; he climbed Mount Safa and called the clans of Quraysh, asking if they would believe him if he warned of an army behind the hill; they said yes as he had always been truthful; he then warned them of a severe punishment; Abu Lahab cursed him and Sura 111 was revealed about Abu Lahab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of the migrations of Muslims to Abyssinia.
parts.answer: In the fifth year of prophethood (about 615 CE), because of persecution, the Prophet (pbuh) allowed a small group, including 'Uthman and his wife Ruqayya, to go to Abyssinia, ruled by a just Christian king, the Negus; a larger group followed under Ja'far bin Abi Talib; the Quraysh sent 'Amr bin al-'As and 'Abdullah bin Abi Rabi'a with gifts to have them returned; the Negus called the Muslims; Ja'far explained Islam and recited from Sura Maryam; the Negus was moved, refused to hand them over and allowed them to live in safety.

parts.text: Give an account of the Prophet's (pbuh) visit to Ta'if.
parts.answer: After the Year of Sorrow he went to Ta'if with Zayd bin Haritha to invite the Thaqif tribe to Islam; its leaders rejected him rudely and set street boys and slaves on him, who threw stones until he was bleeding; he sheltered in a garden and prayed to God, complaining of his weakness but seeking only God's pleasure; Addas, a Christian servant, brought him grapes and accepted his message; Jibril came with the angel of the mountains, offering to crush the people between two mountains, but he refused, hoping their descendants would worship God.

parts.text: Write about the boycott of the Banu Hashim and the 'Year of Sorrow'.

parts.answer: He bought land from two orphans and built the mosque with simple materials, working himself carrying bricks; it served as a place of prayer, teaching, government and shelter for poor Companions (the people of the Suffa); he paired each Emigrant with a Helper as brothers; the Ansar shared homes, property and work; for example Sa'd bin al-Rabi' offered half his wealth to 'Abdur Rahman bin 'Awf, who asked only to be shown the market.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the main terms of the Constitution (Charter) of Madina.
parts.answer: The Muslims (Emigrants and Helpers) formed one community; the Jewish tribes and other groups living in Madina were part of the alliance; each group had freedom of religion; all would defend Madina together against attack and share the costs of war; no one would ally with the Quraysh; disputes would be referred to God and the Prophet (pbuh); Madina was declared a sacred, protected place; blood money and ransom customs would continue fairly within each group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the terms of the Treaty of Hudaybiyya and what happened in the two years after it.
parts.answer: Terms: no fighting for ten years; the Muslims would return to Madina that year and come for pilgrimage the next year for three days, carrying only sheathed swords; any Makkan who went to Madina without his guardian's permission would be returned, but a Muslim going to Makka would not be; tribes could ally with either side. Afterwards, peace allowed many people to learn about and accept Islam; the Muslims performed the lesser pilgrimage the following year; letters were sent to rulers; and in 8 AH the treaty was broken by allies of the Quraysh, leading to the conquest of Makka.

parts.answer: Faith can be strengthened by thinking and observing creation; created things are limited and cannot be God; believers should be prepared to stand against wrong beliefs around them with courage.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed points, e.g.: using reason and observation to strengthen faith, e.g. studying astronomy (1+1); anything that changes or disappears, including wealth or fame, cannot be worthy of worship (1); courage to hold to the truth even when family or society believe otherwise (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the favours and miracles that God mentions in Sura 5.110 regarding the Prophet Jesus.
parts.answer: God reminds Jesus son of Mary of His favour on him and his mother; strengthened him with the Holy Spirit; he spoke to people in the cradle and as an adult; he was taught the Book, wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel; by God's permission he made a bird of clay that became a living bird, healed the blind and the leper and brought the dead to life; God held back the Children of Israel from harming him when they called his miracles magic.
parts.working: Indicative content: Favour on Jesus and on his mother Mary; support with the Holy Spirit (Jibril); speaking in the cradle and in maturity; taught writing / the Book and wisdom; taught the Torah and the Gospel; shaped a bird of clay and breathed into it and it became a bird, by God's leave; healed those born blind and lepers, by God's leave; raised the dead, by God's leave; protected from the Children of Israel who said his signs were magic. parts.answer: It shows that the miracles came from God's power, not Jesus's own, so Jesus is honoured as a great prophet but is a human servant of God, not divine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the themes of Sura 108 (al-Kawthar).
parts.answer: God has given the Prophet (pbuh) abundant good (al-Kawthar); in thanks he should pray to his Lord and offer sacrifice; it is his enemy who will be cut off, not him.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: God has granted the Prophet (pbuh) abundance / al-Kawthar (a river or great blessing in Paradise); God's generosity and care for His messenger; so pray to God alone; and sacrifice for Him alone; worship and sacrifice should be sincere for God; the one who hates / mocks the Prophet (pbuh) will be the one cut off; reassurance against those who said he had no lasting legacy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the message of this sura can encourage Muslims who are mocked for their faith.
parts.answer: God's support is greater than people's insults; Muslims should respond with prayer, thankfulness and good character rather than anger, trusting that truth lasts and mockery fades.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed points, e.g.: God honoured the Prophet (pbuh) when he was mocked, so believers are not truly harmed by insults (1); respond by worship and gratitude rather than revenge (1); example, e.g. a student mocked for praying at school continues calmly (1); those who oppose truth lose in the end — patience is rewarded (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main themes of Sura 112 (al-Ikhlas).
parts.answer: God is One and unique; He is eternal and absolute, needing nothing while all depend on Him; He has no children and no parents; nothing is comparable to Him.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a Muslim can show belief in the teaching of this sura in daily life.
parts.answer: By worshipping and relying on God alone, avoiding anything that gives His position to another, and treating all people as equal servants of the one God.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 per relevant action, +1 for developing it with a reason or example. parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about what Sura 2.255 (Ayat al-Kursi) teaches about God's power and knowledge.
parts.answer: God is ever-living and sustains everything; He never tires or sleeps; He owns all that is in the heavens and earth; no one can intercede with Him except by His permission; He knows everything past and future while people know only what He allows; His authority covers the heavens and earth and guarding them does not tire Him; He is the Most High, the Supreme.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the themes of Sura 6.101–103.
parts.answer: God is the Originator of the heavens and earth; He cannot have a son as He has no partner; He created everything and knows everything; He alone deserves worship and takes care of all affairs; no vision can grasp Him but He sees all; He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The passage says that no human vision can grasp God. Explain how this teaching should affect the way Muslims think about God.
parts.answer: Muslims should not picture God as a created form or make images of Him; they understand Him through His names, attributes and signs, while knowing He sees them at all times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what each of the following passages teaches about God: (i) Sura 41.37, (ii) Sura 42.4–5.
parts.answer: (i) Night, day, sun and moon are signs of God; people should not prostrate to the sun or moon but only to God who created them. parts.answer: Sura 112: God is One, self-sufficient, neither begets nor was begotten, and nothing is like Him. 6.101–103: as Originator of everything He has no consort and so no son; He is Creator of all and beyond sight.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how belief in God's uniqueness can help a Muslim living in a multi-faith city such as Toronto or Karachi to relate to people of other faiths.
parts.answer: It gives the Muslim a clear identity in belief while reminding them that all people are God's creation, so they can live respectfully and justly alongside others without compromising their faith.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how 'Umar became caliph and the attitude he showed at the start of his caliphate.
parts.answer: During his final illness in 13 AH (634 CE) Abu Bakr consulted senior Companions such as 'Abdur Rahman bin 'Awf and 'Uthman about 'Umar; some worried about his strictness, but Abu Bakr said responsibility would soften him; he had his nomination written down by 'Uthman and read to the people, who accepted it and gave their pledge; 'Umar was known as al-Faruq and became the first to be called Amir al-Mu'minin; in his first address he said he would be gentle with the good and firm with wrongdoers, asked people to correct him and promised to serve them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the main administrative reforms introduced by 'Umar.
parts.answer: He divided the empire into provinces run by governors; appointed judges (qadis) separate from governors; organised the treasury (bayt al-mal); set up the diwan, a register for paying stipends to soldiers and citizens; introduced the Hijri calendar; built garrison towns such as Basra, Kufa and Fustat; organised a police and army system with regular pay; carried out land surveys and kept conquered land under state control for revenue; dug canals and built roads; set up guest houses and helped the poor and elderly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the conquest of the Persian Empire during 'Umar's caliphate.
parts.answer: Under Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas the Muslims defeated a large Persian army at the Battle of Qadisiyya (about 636 CE), where the Persian general Rustam was killed; they captured the Persian capital al-Mada'in (Ctesiphon) with its treasures; further victories followed, such as Jalula; the decisive Battle of Nihawand (about 642 CE), under Nu'man bin Muqarrin, who was martyred, broke Persian power and was called the 'victory of victories'.

parts.text: Give an account of the martyrdom of 'Umar and the arrangements he made for choosing his successor.
parts.answer: In 23 AH (644 CE), while leading the dawn prayer in the Prophet's mosque, 'Umar was stabbed several times by Abu Lu'lu'a Fayruz, a Persian slave who held a grudge; 'Abdur Rahman bin 'Awf completed the prayer; 'Umar asked who had attacked him and thanked God that it was not a Muslim who prayed; he asked 'A'isha for permission to be buried beside the Prophet (pbuh) and Abu Bakr; he appointed a council of six — 'Uthman, 'Ali, 'Abdur Rahman bin 'Awf, Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas, al-Zubayr and Talha — to choose a caliph within three days; his son 'Abdullah could advise but not be chosen; he died three days later.

parts.text: Describe how 'Umar treated non-Muslims living in the Muslim state.

parts.answer: Abu Bakr consulted Companions about the apostates and the compilation of the Qur'an, and about nominating 'Umar; 'Umar had a council of senior Companions, consulted them on matters such as the conquered lands and the calendar, and appointed the council of six; 'Uthman consulted Companions on the standard copy of the Qur'an; 'Ali consulted his supporters before major decisions and on accepting arbitration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the ways in which Abu Bakr and 'Ali dealt with groups who opposed the authority of the state.
parts.answer: Abu Bakr faced tribes who refused zakat and false prophets; he insisted zakat was part of Islam, sent eleven armies and defeated them, e.g. at Yamama. 'Ali faced opposition from Muslims over 'Uthman's killers and from the Kharijites; he tried negotiation before the Camel, accepted arbitration at Siffin and debated the Kharijites, fighting at Nahrawan only after they killed innocent people. Both acted to protect the unity of the state; Abu Bakr was dealing mainly with rebellion against Islam's obligations, while 'Ali faced civil conflict among Muslims.

Comparison: similarities — both defended the unity of the state and used force when necessary; differences — the nature of the opponents (apostates vs fellow Muslims), and 'Ali's greater use of negotiation. parts.label: a
parts.text: Give an account of the martyrdom of any two of the following: 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali.
parts.answer: 'Umar: stabbed during Fajr in the Prophet's mosque in 23 AH by Abu Lu'lu'a; appointed the council of six; buried beside the Prophet (pbuh) and Abu Bakr. 'Ali: struck by the Kharijite ibn Muljam with a poisoned sword during the dawn prayer in Kufa in 40 AH; he forbade cruelty to his attacker and died two days later.

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that every action is valued according to the intention behind it, and each person receives the result of what they truly meant to do.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Deeds are judged by the intention in the heart; God rewards sincerity, so the same outward act can be worthy or worthless depending on its purpose; a believer's actions should be done for God's pleasure.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: intention (niyya) is the basis of every deed; God knows what is in the heart; reward depends on sincerity, not outward appearance; good acts done for show or worldly gain lose their reward; ordinary acts can become worship with a good intention; each person is responsible for their own intention.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Muslims can put this teaching into practice in their daily lives.
parts.answer: By renewing a sincere intention before actions — study, work, charity, worship — so that they are done for God rather than praise, and by checking their motives.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 per practical action, +1 for development, e.g.: giving charity quietly rather than posting about it online (1+1); studying with the intention of serving the community makes study an act of worship (1+1); making intention before prayer and fasting (1); self-checking motives when helping others (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that God does not look at people's bodies, looks or wealth; rather He looks at their hearts and their deeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What does this Hadith teach Muslims about how God judges people?
parts.answer: God judges by inner faith, sincerity and actions, not by appearance, race, wealth or status; all people are equal before Him and differ only in piety and deeds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: outward appearance is not the basis of God's judgement; wealth and status do not earn God's favour; God sees the heart / intentions; deeds matter; equality of all people; piety (taqwa) is the true measure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can Muslims act on this teaching in a society that values looks and money? Give examples.
parts.answer: By treating people equally whatever their appearance or income, focusing on improving their own character rather than image, and not judging others by clothes or wealth.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed examples, e.g.: respecting a cleaner or driver as much as a rich guest (1+1); not judging classmates by brands or phones (1); spending more effort on good deeds than on appearance or social-media image (1+1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that true richness does not come from having many possessions; real richness is contentment of the soul.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Wealth is not measured by possessions but by contentment; a person who is satisfied with what God has given is truly rich, while a greedy person stays poor however much he has.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: material wealth does not bring real richness; contentment (qana'a) is true wealth; greed leaves a person always wanting more; gratitude for God's provision; inner peace matters more than possessions; wealth is a test from God.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this teaching could help a young Muslim today.
parts.answer: It helps them avoid comparison and envy, especially on social media, spend wisely, be grateful and find peace in faith and relationships rather than possessions.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed points, e.g.: not envying friends' expensive phones or holidays (1+1); avoiding debt and wasteful spending (1); valuing family, faith and good deeds above possessions (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that purity (cleanliness) is half of faith.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Cleanliness of body, clothes and surroundings, and purity of the heart, are a central part of faith; physical purity is needed for worship, and inner purity means freedom from sin and bad intentions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: cleanliness is a major part of faith; physical purity — body, clothes, place; wudu and ghusl are needed for prayer; inner purity — heart free of pride, envy and sin; cleanliness pleases God; hygiene protects health.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can Muslims put this teaching into practice at home and in their community?
parts.answer: By keeping themselves and their homes clean, performing wudu carefully, keeping streets, mosques and public places free of litter and working on purifying their character.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed examples, e.g.: regular washing and clean clothes (1); careful wudu before prayer (1); community clean-up days in a neighbourhood in Lahore or a park in Manchester (1+1); purifying the heart from envy and grudges (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): When asked about the highest level of faith, the Prophet (pbuh) explained that it is to worship God as though you can see Him, and although you cannot see Him, to know that He certainly sees you.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith about ihsan (excellence in faith).
parts.answer: Ihsan is the highest level of faith: worshipping with full awareness of God's presence, as if seeing Him; since He sees everything, the believer acts sincerely and carefully in public and private.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: ihsan is the highest stage of religion (after islam and iman); worship with complete focus and devotion; awareness that God is always watching; this produces sincerity and humility; excellence in all actions, not only prayer; part of the well-known Hadith in which Jibril questioned the Prophet (pbuh).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this teaching can improve a Muslim's prayer and behaviour.
parts.answer: Awareness of God's presence brings concentration and humility in prayer, and makes the believer honest and careful even when no one else is watching.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: focus and calm in salat, avoiding rushing or distraction by the phone (1+1); honesty in private, e.g. not cheating in an online test (1); doing work to the best standard because God sees it (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): A man asked the Prophet (pbuh) whether he should leave his camel untied and trust in God, or tie it and trust in God. The Prophet (pbuh) told him to tie it and then trust in God.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Trust in God (tawakkul) does not mean doing nothing; a Muslim must take sensible practical steps and then rely on God for the result.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: tawakkul is part of faith; it must be combined with effort; people must take reasonable precautions; the result is in God's hands; laziness is not trust; balance between action and reliance on God.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of how a Muslim can act on this Hadith today, explaining each.
parts.answer: E.g. a student revises thoroughly and then prays for success, accepting the result; a family in a flood-prone area in Sindh prepares and follows warnings while trusting God; a traveller locks the car and trusts God.
parts.working: 2 marks per example: 1 for the action (effort / precaution), 1 for explaining how trust in God is added (prayer, calm acceptance of outcome).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that none of you truly has faith until he wants for his brother what he wants for himself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Complete faith includes caring for others; a believer should wish good for others as for himself, avoid jealousy and selfishness, and see other believers as brothers and sisters.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: faith is not complete without love for others; wish the same good for others as for yourself; removes envy and selfishness; brotherhood / sisterhood among believers; many scholars extend this to all humanity; faith shown in attitudes and conduct towards others.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can Muslims show this teaching in action? Give examples.
parts.answer: By sharing, helping others succeed, being happy at their success and treating others as they would like to be treated.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed examples, e.g.: sharing notes with a classmate before exams instead of hiding them (1+1); congratulating a colleague's promotion without envy (1); giving good-quality items in charity, the kind one would want oneself (1+1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that whoever believes in God and the Last Day should either say something good or remain silent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about the link between belief and speech.
parts.answer: Belief in God and the Day of Judgement should show in how a Muslim speaks; since words are recorded and will be judged, the believer speaks only what is good and otherwise stays silent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: true faith affects behaviour; speech is an important part of conduct; belief in the Last Day — words will be accounted for; say only what is good, true and useful; avoid lies, backbiting, insults, gossip; silence is better than harmful speech.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can Muslims apply this teaching to their use of social media?
parts.answer: By posting and commenting only what is true and beneficial, not spreading rumours or insulting people, and staying silent rather than joining arguments or gossip.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: checking facts before sharing (1+1); avoiding hurtful comments, mockery or backbiting online (1); using platforms to spread useful knowledge or kindness (1); stepping away from heated arguments (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that God divided mercy into one hundred parts; He kept ninety-nine with Himself and sent down one part to the earth, and it is from that one part that all creatures show mercy to one another, even an animal lifting its hoof so as not to harm its young.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about God's mercy.
parts.answer: God's mercy is immense, far greater than all the mercy found in creation; every act of kindness on earth comes from a small portion of it; He keeps the greater share for His servants in the Hereafter, which gives hope of forgiveness.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: mercy is one of God's greatest attributes; all compassion in creation comes from Him; the mercy seen on earth is only a tiny share; ninety-nine parts are kept for the Day of Judgement; even animals' care for their young is from God's mercy; believers should never despair of God's mercy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Knowing that God is so merciful may make people careless about sin.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: Disagree mostly: God's mercy should lead to gratitude, hope and repentance rather than carelessness; Muslims balance hope in mercy with fear of accountability, and mercy also calls them to be merciful to others.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: a clear judgement (1); mercy brings hope and encourages repentance, not complacency (1); balance of hope and fear / accountability on the Day of Judgement (1); believers are expected to reflect this mercy to others, with example (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) said that a hypocrite has three signs: when he speaks he lies, when he makes a promise he breaks it, and when he is trusted he betrays the trust.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about the qualities expected of a true believer.
parts.answer: A believer's faith must be matched by honesty, keeping promises and faithfulness to trusts; lying, breaking promises and betraying trust are signs of hypocrisy, where outward faith hides an inner fault.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: faith must be shown in character; truthfulness is essential; promises must be kept; trusts (amanah) must be honoured, including property, secrets and responsibilities; these three faults are signs of hypocrisy (nifaq); a believer should examine himself for them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: To what extent is keeping promises the most important of these three qualities in modern society? Give reasons.
parts.answer: A reasoned judgement, e.g. all three are linked — business contracts, family commitments and public office all depend on promises, but honesty underlies keeping promises and trusts, so truthfulness may be the foundation.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: judgement (1); reasoned support for promises, e.g. contracts, deadlines, marriage (1); comparison with truthfulness or trust, e.g. public officials handling funds (1); modern example and conclusion (1).

practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that this world is like a prison for the believer and like a paradise for the disbeliever.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: The believer restrains desires and follows God's limits in this life, so it feels restricting compared with the reward awaiting him; the disbeliever treats this world as his only enjoyment, and it is the best he will have compared with what follows; this life is temporary and a test.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: this world is temporary; it is a test; the believer accepts limits set by God (lawful and unlawful); the believer's true home and reward are in the Hereafter; compared with Paradise, worldly life is restricted; for one who rejects the Hereafter, worldly pleasure is all there is; it does not mean believers must be unhappy or reject lawful enjoyment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this teaching can help Muslims cope with hardship and temptation.
parts.answer: It reminds them that difficulties and self-restraint are temporary and will be rewarded, so they stay patient in hardship and resist temptations that bring short pleasure but long regret.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: patience in illness, poverty or loss knowing it is temporary (1+1); resisting unlawful income or pleasures by keeping the Hereafter in mind (1+1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that the strong person is not the one who defeats others in wrestling; the strong person is the one who controls himself when he is angry.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Real strength is self-control, not physical power; a Muslim should control anger and not act on it through violence or harsh words.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: true strength is moral / inner strength; physical strength is not the measure of a person; anger must be controlled; acting in anger leads to harm and regret; self-discipline is a sign of faith; patience is praised in Islam.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain practical ways a Muslim can act on this Hadith.
parts.answer: By staying calm in arguments, keeping quiet, changing position, making wudu, seeking refuge in God from Satan and forgiving others.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: 1 per method, +1 for development, e.g.: staying silent or walking away during a quarrel (1+1); sitting down if standing, making wudu (1); seeking refuge in God (1); calm driving in Karachi traffic instead of road rage (1+1); forgiving instead of taking revenge (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that whoever among you sees something wrong should change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; and if he cannot, then in his heart, and that is the weakest level of faith.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Muslims have a duty to oppose wrong in the way they are able: by action if they have the authority, by speaking out if not, and at least by hating it in the heart; it is part of faith to care about wrongdoing in society.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: duty to forbid wrong; three levels — action, speech, heart; according to one's ability and authority; changing by hand means proper action by those responsible, not violence by individuals; disliking wrong in the heart is the minimum; faith is linked to social responsibility.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of how a Muslim today can act on this Hadith at different levels.
parts.answer: E.g. a teacher stops bullying in her class (hand); a student speaks up politely when friends mock someone (tongue); a person who cannot act stays away from a gathering where backbiting takes place and prays for change (heart).
parts.working: 2 marks per example: 1 for a suitable wrong and action, 1 for linking it to the correct level and to the person's ability.

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that smiling at your brother is an act of charity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Charity is not only giving money; simple kind acts such as a smile are rewarded; Muslims should be cheerful and friendly, spreading happiness and brotherhood.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: charity (sadaqa) has many forms; even small acts are rewarded; a smile spreads love and goodwill; it costs nothing, so everyone can give; good manners are part of faith; strengthens brotherhood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Muslims can act on this teaching in a busy city such as Karachi or New York.
parts.answer: By greeting neighbours, shopkeepers and colleagues warmly, welcoming newcomers at the mosque and being cheerful with family, which builds friendship in places where people often feel isolated.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed examples: greeting and smiling at colleagues and staff (1+1); welcoming new students or neighbours (1); positive manner with family after a stressful day (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for those in his care: the ruler for his people, a man for his family, a woman for her husband's home and children, and a servant for his master's property.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Everyone has responsibilities over others or over trusts given to them, and will be asked about how they carried them out; this applies to rulers, parents, spouses and workers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: everyone is a guardian / shepherd; responsibility is a trust (amanah); rulers responsible for citizens; husbands for families; wives for the home and children; employees for property in their care; all will be questioned by God; no one is without responsibility.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this Hadith can guide two different people in Pakistan today, such as a government official and a parent.
parts.answer: The official must serve citizens honestly, avoid corruption and use public funds properly; the parent must provide, educate and give a good example to children, knowing both will be asked by God.
parts.working: 2 marks per person: 1 for a relevant responsibility, 1 for development (e.g. official — fair service, no bribes; parent — religious and academic education, time and love).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that God is gentle and loves gentleness in every matter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Gentleness is one of God's qualities and He loves it in people; Muslims should be kind and soft in manner in all situations, avoiding harshness, which spoils things.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: gentleness (rifq) is loved by God; it applies to all matters; harshness is disliked; gentleness achieves what harshness cannot; it is part of good character; the Prophet (pbuh) himself was gentle with people.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Muslims can show gentleness in family life and at work.
parts.answer: By speaking softly to children and elderly parents, correcting mistakes kindly, being patient with colleagues and customers and treating animals with care.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed examples: correcting a child's mistake calmly rather than shouting (1+1); patience with ageing parents (1); a manager giving feedback respectfully (1); kindness to animals (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) instructed that a worker should be given his wages before his sweat has dried.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Employers must pay workers fully and promptly; delaying wages is injustice; workers' rights and dignity must be respected; fair dealing is part of faith.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: pay wages promptly; pay the full agreed amount; delay or cheating is oppression; respect the dignity of labour; workers depend on wages for their families; fairness in business is required by Islam.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can this Hadith be put into practice by employers today?
parts.answer: By paying salaries on time, honouring agreed wages, giving fair pay to domestic workers and daily-wage labourers, and providing safe working conditions.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: monthly salaries paid on the agreed date (1); daily labourers in construction paid at the end of the day (1); fair wages and no unfair deductions for domestic workers (1+1); safe conditions and respect (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that the believers, in their love, mercy and kindness towards one another, are like one body: when one part is in pain, the whole body suffers with sleeplessness and fever.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Muslims form one community bound by love and mercy; they should feel each other's suffering and respond to help; unity and care for others are signs of faith.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: unity of the ummah; mutual love, mercy and compassion; sharing in each other's pain; responsibility to help those suffering; the community is weakened if any member suffers; selfishness has no place among believers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Muslims can act on this teaching when people are suffering in another part of the world or in their own city.
parts.answer: By giving money and supplies to relief efforts, praying for those affected, volunteering locally, and raising awareness, as Muslims did after floods in Pakistan or the earthquake in Türkiye.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for developed points: donations to disaster relief (1+1); volunteering locally, e.g. food for the homeless (1); prayer and raising awareness (1); visiting the sick in one's own community (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that a true Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand other people are safe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Being a Muslim means not harming others by words or actions; faith shows in the safety and peace others feel around you.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: Islam means peace / safety; the tongue can harm through lies, insults and backbiting; the hand can harm through violence, theft or cheating; a believer must not harm others; good conduct is a sign of true faith; this includes harm through writing / online.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of how a Muslim can act on this Hadith today, explaining each.
parts.answer: E.g. refusing to join in mocking someone in a WhatsApp group (tongue); driving carefully and not damaging public property (hand).
parts.working: 2 marks per example: 1 for the action, 1 for showing how it keeps others safe from harm by tongue or hand.

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that faith has many branches; the highest is to declare that there is no god but God, the lowest is to remove something harmful from the road, and modesty is also a branch of faith.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what this Hadith teaches about the nature of faith.
parts.answer: Faith is not only belief but includes many actions, from the declaration of God's oneness to small public services; even removing an obstacle from a path is part of faith, and good character such as modesty is included.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: faith (iman) has many parts / branches; belief in tawhid is the highest; small acts of service are also faith; caring for public safety is part of religion; modesty (haya') is a branch; faith covers belief, speech and action.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the importance of small acts, such as removing harm from a road, in a Muslim's faith.
parts.answer: They are very important because they show faith in everyday life, protect others and are rewarded; but they should come with correct belief, the highest branch, so both together make complete faith.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: judgement (1); small acts protect the community — e.g. removing glass from a road, reporting an open manhole (1); they keep faith active every day (1); balanced against belief and obligatory worship (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) instructed his followers to make things easy and not difficult for people, and to give good news and not drive people away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Islam is a religion of ease; Muslims should present faith positively, avoid making religion harsh or burdensome and encourage people with hope rather than fear and blame.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: make things easy; do not make religion hard for others; give glad tidings / be positive; do not repel people by harshness; teaching should be gentle and encouraging; applies to teachers, preachers, parents and leaders.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A new Muslim in London finds some members of the mosque critical of her mistakes in prayer. Explain how the community should act on this Hadith.
parts.answer: They should teach her gently and patiently, praise her efforts, introduce practices step by step and make her feel welcome so she is encouraged rather than driven away.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: gentle correction in private (1); encouragement and praise for effort (1); gradual teaching — essentials first (1); welcoming support such as classes or a friend to guide her (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths: putting teachings into action
practice.stem: Hadith (meaning in plain English): The Prophet (pbuh) taught that the upper hand is better than the lower hand: the upper hand is the one that gives, and the lower hand is the one that receives.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the teaching of this Hadith.
parts.answer: Giving is better than receiving; Muslims should work to support themselves and others, be generous, and avoid begging when they can earn; but it does not look down on genuine need.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: generosity is praised; giving is more honourable than taking; encourages hard work and self-reliance; discourages begging without need; wealth is to be shared; those in genuine need still have a right to help; giving should be done with dignity for the receiver.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A young man in Lahore can work but relies on relatives for money. Evaluate how this Hadith applies to his situation.
parts.answer: He should seek work and become self-reliant so he can support himself and later help others; relatives may help in the short term, and if he truly cannot work, accepting help is not shameful; the aim is to become a giver.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: judgement (1); encourages him to earn and avoid dependence (1); recognises genuine hardship / temporary help is allowed (1); aims to become a giver — family, charity (1).

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths essay: personal and communal guidance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using Hadiths you have studied, describe how Muslims should treat other people.
parts.answer: Wish for others what you wish for yourself; keep others safe from your tongue and hand; be gentle; smile, which is charity; show mercy; make things easy; speak good or stay silent; pay workers promptly.
parts.working: Indicative content: Relevant teachings, each correctly linked to the meaning of a set Hadith (not just listed), e.g.: love for your brother what you love for yourself; speak good or stay silent; honour your neighbour and guest; mercy to others brings God's mercy; a Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand others are safe; control anger; be kind and gentle. Answers using only one or two Hadiths cannot go above Level 2; Hadiths must be linked to behaviour, not just quoted. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why good treatment of others is an important part of a Muslim's faith.
parts.answer: Because the Hadiths link faith directly to conduct, so treating people well is worship and its absence weakens faith.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Link between faith and conduct, development (e.g. 'none of you believes until…'). Model answer: Because the Hadiths link faith directly to conduct, so treating people well is worship and its absence weakens faith. Marked by levels out of 4. Level 4 (4): a well-developed, reasoned answer (two developed points, or one fully developed point) linked to life today, with a clear judgement where the question asks for one. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths essay: personal and communal guidance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the Hadiths, describe how a young Muslim should behave at school or college.
parts.answer: Study with a good intention; control anger in arguments; speak good or stay silent; do not harm others with words or actions, including bullying; be gentle and smile at others; be honest — avoid lies and broken promises; wish for classmates what you want for yourself.
parts.working: Indicative content: Relevant behaviours linked to Hadiths, e.g.: seek knowledge; good intention in studying; honesty — no cheating, since the signs of a hypocrite include lying; speak good or stay silent; control anger; kindness and respect to teachers and classmates; love for others what you love for yourself; cleanliness; perseverance. Behaviours must be linked to Hadiths and applied to school or college for Level 3 and above. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how one of these teachings could change the atmosphere of a school.
parts.answer: For example, if students kept others safe from their tongues and hands, bullying and fights would reduce and everyone would feel secure.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Chosen teaching, explaining its effect on the school. Model answer: For example, if students kept others safe from their tongues and hands, bullying and fights would reduce and everyone would feel secure. Marked by levels out of 4. Level 4 (4): a well-developed, reasoned answer (two developed points, or one fully developed point) linked to life today, with a clear judgement where the question asks for one. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths essay: personal and communal guidance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the guidance that the Hadiths give for family life.
parts.answer: Each person is a shepherd responsible for those in his care — parents for children, spouses for the home; gentleness is loved by God in every matter; anger should be controlled; good speech or silence; mercy to others brings God's mercy; smiling is charity — warmth at home; intentions make daily duties acts of worship.
parts.working: Indicative content: Relevant points linked to Hadiths, e.g.: the best of you are those best to their families; kindness to wives; respect and service to parents, especially the mother; mercy to children and respect for elders; maintaining ties of kinship; provision for the family as charity; good character at home. At least three different Hadiths are needed for Level 4. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which of these teachings do you think would most improve family life today? Give a reason.
parts.answer: A reasoned choice, e.g. controlling anger, because many family conflicts begin with harsh words.
parts.working: Mark points to credit: Judgement, developed reason. Model answer: A reasoned choice, e.g. controlling anger, because many family conflicts begin with harsh words. Marked by levels out of 4. Level 4 (4): a well-developed, reasoned answer (two developed points, or one fully developed point) linked to life today, with a clear judgement where the question asks for one. Level 3 (3): a reasoned answer with some development and a relevant example, but the judgement or link to today is less clear. Level 2 (2): one or two simple points with little development. Level 1 (1): a basic, general statement. 0: nothing creditworthy.

practice.subtopic: Set Hadiths essay: personal and communal guidance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the Hadiths, describe how a Muslim should control his or her own self (nafs).
parts.answer: Control anger — real strength; guard the tongue — speak good or stay silent; check intentions; avoid lying, breaking promises and betraying trust; be content rather than greedy; keep pure in body and heart; remember God sees you.
parts.working: Indicative content: Points linked to Hadiths, e.g.: the strong man is the one who controls himself when angry; speak good or remain silent; actions are judged by intentions; the signs of a hypocrite (lying, breaking promises, betraying trust); true richness is richness of the soul; purity is half of faith; ihsan — worship God as if you see Him. Points must be linked to Hadiths; several different Hadiths are needed for Level 3 and above. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. parts.label: a
parts.text: The Sunna includes the sayings, actions and silent approval of the Prophet (pbuh). Explain each of these, giving an example.
parts.answer: Sayings: his words teaching or commanding, e.g. his teaching that actions are judged by intentions. Actions: what he did, which Companions observed and copied, e.g. how he performed prayer, wudu and hajj. Silent approval: something done in his presence or known to him which he did not object to, showing it is allowed, e.g. Companions eating a desert lizard in front of him although he himself did not eat it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe ijma' (consensus) as a source of Islamic law and explain how it is linked to the Qur'an and Hadith.
parts.answer: Ijma' is the agreement of the qualified scholars of the community (first the Companions) on a ruling after the Prophet's death; it is used where the Qur'an and Hadith are not explicit; it gets its authority from the Qur'an's command to obey those in authority and to hold together and not divide, and from the Hadith that the community will not agree on an error; it must be based on and agree with the Qur'an and Sunna; an example is the Companions' agreement to collect the Qur'an into one book.

Hajj: the Qur'an commands hajj and mentions some rites; the Prophet (pbuh) performed it in front of the Companions and told them to learn their rites from him, so the order and details of the rites (ihram, tawaf, standing at 'Arafa, stoning) come from his practice.

parts.text: Explain the differences between the Qur'an, a Hadith Qudsi and an ordinary (Prophetic) Hadith.
parts.answer: The Qur'an: God's own words, both meaning and wording, revealed through Jibril, recited in prayer, preserved in one text, and transmitted by vast numbers. A Prophetic Hadith: the Prophet's own words, actions or approvals, guided by God but not reported as God speaking; its authenticity varies and is graded by scholars.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the instructions given by the Prophet (pbuh) about how his Hadiths should be passed on accurately.
parts.answer: He warned that anyone who deliberately lies about him will take his place in Hell; he prayed for the one who hears his words, memorises them and passes them on exactly as heard; he told those present to convey to those absent; Companions such as 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr were allowed to write his words; Companions were careful, some reporting little for fear of error.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: warning against lying about him; prayer for those who convey accurately; present to inform absent; permission to write (example); Companions' caution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some of the closest Companions, such as Abu Bakr and 'Umar, narrated far fewer Hadiths than younger Companions such as Abu Hurayra and Ibn 'Abbas. Suggest reasons for this and what it shows about their attitude to the Hadiths.
parts.answer: They feared making a mistake and so falsely attributing words to the Prophet (pbuh), in view of his warning; they were busy leading and governing the community; they died earlier, before later generations came seeking Hadiths, while younger Companions lived longer and taught many students; 'Umar also discouraged too much narration so that people would concentrate on the Qur'an. It shows deep respect for the Prophet's words and a strong sense of responsibility for accuracy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how scholars identified a fabricated (mawdu') Hadith.
parts.answer: A narrator in the chain was a known liar or admitted forging; the chain was broken or the narrators could not have met (dates and places did not match); the report was known only from one unreliable narrator; the text contradicted the Qur'an, authentic Sunna or established facts; the language was weak or unlike the Prophet's style; it contained extreme rewards or threats for trivial acts; it clearly served the interest of a sect, ruler, tribe or trade.
parts.working: Indicative content: Isnad signs: a known liar or unknown narrator in the chain; a narrator who could not have met his source; a report found only from one unreliable source. Matn signs: contradicts the Qur'an or mutawatir Hadith; huge rewards for tiny deeds; poor or un-Prophetic language; favours a sect, ruler or tribe; contradicts reason or known history; the fabricator's confession. Both isnad and matn signs are needed for Level 4. Marked by levels out of 10. Level 4 (9–10): a full, accurate and well-organised answer with precise detail (names, dates, places, sequence) and supporting references to the Qur'an or Hadith where relevant. Level 3 (6–8): a mostly accurate answer covering the main points, with some detail but gaps or little supporting evidence. Level 2 (3–5): a general answer with some relevant points but limited detail or some errors. Level 1 (1–2): a few basic or partly relevant points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: To what extent were these methods successful in protecting the Sunna? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Largely successful: scholars produced collections of authentic Hadiths and separate books listing fabricated ones, so Muslims can tell them apart; but fabricated sayings still circulate among people who do not check, so education is still needed today.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Hadiths were preserved during the lifetime of the Prophet (pbuh) and the time of the Companions.
parts.answer: Companions memorised his words and observed his actions, often learning in groups and repeating them; at first he discouraged writing Hadiths in case they were confused with the Qur'an, but later some Companions were allowed to write, e.g. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, whose notebook was called al-Sahifa al-Sadiqa; his letters and treaties were kept in writing; after his death Companions such as Abu Hurayra, 'A'isha, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Anas ibn Malik taught many students; they were careful and checked each other's reports; Companions spread to new cities and taught there.
parts.working: Indicative content: Memorisation; practice/observing; early discouragement of writing (reason); later permission; 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr's al-Sahifa al-Sadiqa; written letters/treaties; named Companions who narrated many Hadiths; teaching students; caution/checking; spread to new cities. parts.label: b
parts.text: Why did the Prophet (pbuh) at first discourage writing his sayings?
parts.answer: So that his words would not be mixed up with the Qur'an while it was still being revealed and written; once the Qur'an was well known and distinct, writing was allowed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the stage of Hadith collection in the time of the Successors (Tabi'un), including the role of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz.
parts.answer: As the Companions died and fabrication grew, the need for written collection increased; the Umayyad caliph 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ordered scholars and governors to collect and write down the Hadiths so that they would not be lost; Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri was among the first to collect them on this order; scholars travelled across the Muslim lands to gather reports; collections were often arranged by topic and mixed with sayings of Companions and rulings; Imam Malik's al-Muwatta' in Madina is an early surviving example.

parts.text: Why do you think a ruler's support was important for this stage of collection?
parts.answer: A caliph's order gave the work official backing and resources, encouraged scholars across the provinces to collect and send reports, and made the task urgent before knowledge was lost; but scholars kept their independence in judging Hadiths.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a musnad and a musannaf collection of Hadiths, and give an example of each.
parts.answer: Musnad: Hadiths arranged by the name of the Companion who narrated them, all reports of one Companion together, e.g. the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Musannaf: Hadiths arranged by subject (e.g. purification, prayer, zakat, trade), e.g. the Sahih of al-Bukhari or the Sahih of Muslim.
parts.working: 1 mark: musnad definition; 1 mark: musnad example; 1 mark: musannaf definition; 1 mark: musannaf example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which type of collection would be more useful to a judge needing a ruling on a business contract, and which to a scholar studying the reports of 'A'isha? Explain your answers.
parts.answer: The judge would use a musannaf, because all Hadiths on trade and contracts are found together under one chapter; the scholar would use a musnad, because all the reports narrated by 'A'isha are grouped under her name, making it easy to study her narrations and check them.
parts.working: 2 marks each: correct type (1) and reason (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the 'golden age' of Hadith compilation in the third century after the migration, naming the main collections.
parts.answer: In the third century AH (ninth century CE) scholars produced the most respected collections, using strict methods to check chains and texts; the six main Sunni collections are the Sahih of al-Bukhari, the Sahih of Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, and the Sunan of Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah; al-Bukhari and Muslim included only Hadiths they judged sahih; the Sunan works focused on legal Hadiths and noted the strength of reports; the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal is also from this time. Shi'a Muslims rely mainly on four later collections: al-Kafi (al-Kulayni), Man la yahduruhu al-faqih (al-Saduq), and Tahdhib al-ahkam and al-Istibsar (al-Tusi).
parts.working: Indicative content: Third century AH / ninth century CE; strict criticism methods; the six collections — Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i, Ibn Maja; Bukhari and Muslim include only sahih reports; the Sunan focus on law; the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal; the Shi'a four books (credit as alternative). parts.answer: By then Hadiths were spread in many cities and could be gathered by travel; the science of narrators had developed fully; fabrication had become widespread, so a reliable selection was urgently needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about Imam al-Bukhari and the method he used in compiling his Sahih.
parts.answer: He was born in Bukhara in Central Asia in 810 CE; he showed a remarkable memory from childhood; he travelled widely (Makka, Madina, Iraq, Syria, Egypt) to learn from hundreds of teachers; he is said to have collected hundreds of thousands of reports and selected only about seven thousand (including repeats) for his Sahih over about sixteen years; he accepted a Hadith only if each narrator was reliable and was known to have actually met the one he narrated from; it is reported that he made ablution and prayed before recording each Hadith; he arranged the book by subject; it is regarded by Sunni Muslims as the most authentic book after the Qur'an; he died in 870 CE near Samarqand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the dates in your answer, calculate al-Bukhari's approximate age at death, and explain what his life teaches students about dedication.
parts.answer: About 60 years (870 − 810). His lifelong travel and care show that valuable knowledge requires patience, effort and honesty; students should work steadily and check their work carefully.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about Abu Bakr's support for the Prophet (pbuh) during the Makkan period and the migration to Madina.
parts.answer: He was a close friend and the first free adult man to accept Islam; he brought others to Islam, such as 'Uthman, al-Zubayr, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Talha; he spent his wealth freeing persecuted slaves including Bilal; he confirmed the Night Journey at once when others mocked, earning the title al-Siddiq; he was chosen to accompany the Prophet (pbuh) on the migration and prepared camels; they hid in the cave of Thawr for three nights, where the Qur'an calls him 'the second of two' (Sura 9.40); his family helped (his daughter Asma brought food, his son 'Abdullah brought news).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how 'Umar ibn al-Khattab accepted Islam.
parts.answer: He was a strong opponent of Islam and set out with his sword intending to kill the Prophet (pbuh); on the way he was told that his own sister Fatima and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd had become Muslims; he went to their house, heard recitation, struck his sister; seeing her bleeding and firm he softened and asked to read the page; it contained verses of Sura Ta-Ha; he was deeply moved; he went to the Prophet (pbuh) at the house of al-Arqam and accepted Islam; the Muslims cried 'God is Greatest'.

parts.text: Describe the life of Bilal ibn Rabah.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a Muslim should do if they miss an obligatory prayer.
parts.answer: Perform it (make it up, qada') as soon as they remember or are able, and ask God's forgiveness if it was missed through carelessness.
parts.working: 1 mark: make it up as soon as possible; 1 mark: repent if missed deliberately/carelessly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the five daily prayers were made obligatory.
parts.answer: During the Night Journey and Ascension (al-Isra' wa al-Mi'raj) the Prophet (pbuh) was taken to the heavens; God made prayers obligatory there, first a larger number; on Musa's advice the Prophet (pbuh) asked for a reduction several times until it became five, with the reward of fifty.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: during the Mi'raj; directly from God; originally more; reduced on Musa's advice; five prayers with reward of fifty.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why is prayer described as the pillar most closely linked to a Muslim's faith?
parts.answer: It is the first act of worship a person will be asked about on the Day of Judgement; it is repeated daily, constantly renewing faith; it is the clearest outward sign of being a Muslim; it was given directly in the heavens, showing its special status.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed reason up to 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the call to prayer (adhan) and its importance in the Muslim community.
parts.answer: It is called aloud by the mu'adhdhin before each obligatory prayer; it declares that God is the Greatest, bears witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His Messenger, calls people to come to prayer and to success, and ends by declaring God's greatness and oneness; Bilal was the first mu'adhdhin in Madina; it announces the time of prayer to the community, gathers people to the mosque, publicly declares the message of Islam, and is also whispered into the ear of a newborn baby.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In some cities, mosques coordinate a single call to prayer broadcast at the same moment. Suggest one benefit and one concern a community might discuss about this.
parts.answer: Benefit: avoids overlapping loud calls at slightly different times, gives a clear signal to everyone and reduces noise complaints. Concern: local mosques lose their own mu'adhdhin's role and the personal link with the community, or local prayer times may differ slightly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the benefits of congregational prayer for the Muslim community.
parts.answer: It brings neighbours together five times a day, so people know each other's needs and help one another; rich and poor, employer and worker stand side by side in straight rows, showing equality; following one imam teaches discipline, order and obedience to rightful leadership; the Prophet (pbuh) taught that praying in congregation brings many times more reward than praying alone; the mosque becomes a centre for learning and welfare; it strengthens unity and brotherhood across races and languages.

parts.text: A young professional in Karachi often prays alone at his desk. Explain to him why he might make the effort to pray in congregation when he can.
parts.answer: He would gain the greater reward promised for congregational prayer, meet and support other Muslims, and feel part of the community; it builds discipline and gives a break from work; if a nearby mosque or prayer room is not possible, praying with colleagues in a group is still congregational.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Friday congregational prayer (Jumu'a).
parts.answer: It is held at the time of the midday prayer on Friday and replaces Zuhr for those who attend; the Qur'an tells believers to hurry to the remembrance of God when the call is made on Friday and to leave their trading, and then to disperse and seek God's bounty after the prayer (Sura 62.9–10); it is obligatory on adult men who are resident and able (women may attend); Muslims take a bath, wear clean clothes and perfume and come early; the imam gives a sermon (khutba), in two parts, which worshippers listen to in silence; then two rak'at are prayed in congregation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can the Friday sermon help a Muslim community deal with issues facing it today?
parts.answer: The imam can give guidance on current issues such as honesty in business, drug abuse, care of the environment or helping flood victims; it reaches the whole community each week; it can unite people around shared action and correct misunderstandings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the concessions Islam allows in prayer for a traveller and for a person who is ill.
parts.answer: A traveller on a journey of the required distance may shorten the four-unit prayers (Zuhr, 'Asr, 'Isha) to two units, while Fajr and Maghrib stay the same; travellers may also combine prayers (Zuhr with 'Asr and Maghrib with 'Isha) according to the rules of their school; a sick person who cannot stand may pray sitting, and if unable to sit may pray lying down, using gestures; if water would harm them they may perform tayammum; prayer is never dropped completely while a person is conscious.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: shortening 4-unit prayers to 2; Fajr and Maghrib unchanged; combining prayers; sitting if unable to stand; lying down / gestures; tayammum if water harmful; prayer still required.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many obligatory rak'at a traveller prays in one full day when shortening, and how many fewer this is than the usual 17.
parts.answer: 11 rak'at (2 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 2); 6 fewer than 17.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What do these concessions show about Islam?
parts.answer: That God makes religion easy and does not burden a person beyond their capacity.
parts.working: 1 mark: ease / no undue hardship.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain when a Muslim may perform tayammum and describe how it is done.
parts.answer: It is allowed when water is not available, or not enough for drinking and wudu, or when using water would cause harm through illness or extreme cold; the person makes the intention, strikes clean earth or dust with the palms, and wipes the face and then the hands (Sura 5.6 and 4.43 permit it); it is cancelled when water becomes available or by anything that breaks wudu.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: no water / not enough; illness or harm; intention; strike clean earth/dust; wipe face; wipe hands; Qur'anic basis; ends when water found.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A group of students on a hiking trip in the northern areas of Pakistan run out of water at prayer time. Explain what they should do and what this teaches about prayer.
parts.answer: They should perform tayammum with clean earth and pray on time, facing the qibla as best they can (using a compass or the sun) and may shorten if they qualify as travellers; this shows that prayer must not be missed, and that Islam provides practical ways to keep it in any situation.
parts.working: 1 mark: tayammum; 1 mark: pray on time / find qibla; 1 mark: possible shortening; 1 mark: lesson (prayer never abandoned / Islam is practical).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how regular prayer can change a Muslim's character and behaviour.
parts.answer: The Qur'an says prayer restrains a person from shameful and wrong deeds (Sura 29.45); remembering God five times a day reminds a person they are accountable; regular timings build discipline and punctuality; purity before prayer encourages cleanliness; standing in rows builds humility and equality; asking forgiveness in prayer encourages honesty about faults; patience and prayer are described as sources of help (Sura 2.45).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four developed points (restrains from wrong; accountability; discipline; cleanliness; humility; seeking help through patience and prayer).

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Some people pray regularly but still behave badly, so prayer does not really change people.' Discuss this view.
parts.answer: The fault is not in prayer but in how it is performed: prayer without attention and sincerity has little effect, and the Qur'an condemns those who are heedless of their prayer; when prayed with understanding and humility it does affect behaviour, as the Qur'an promises; so prayer is a powerful means of change but needs sincere effort; a judgement is required.
parts.working: Level marking. 1: simple view. 2: one argument explained. 3: both sides discussed. 4: balanced discussion with reasoned conclusion (role of sincerity/khushu').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the change of the qibla from Jerusalem to the Ka'ba.
parts.answer: In Makka and for the first months in Madina the Muslims prayed facing Jerusalem; about sixteen to seventeen months after the migration, verses were revealed telling the Prophet (pbuh) to turn his face towards the Sacred Mosque in Makka (Sura 2.144); the Prophet (pbuh) had hoped for this; some Muslims who heard the news turned during their prayer; opponents criticised the change, and the Qur'an answered that East and West belong to God and that the change was a test of who follows the Messenger.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: first qibla Jerusalem; change about 16–17 months after hijra; Qur'anic command (2.144); Prophet's wish; Muslims turned during prayer; criticism answered (East and West belong to God); a test of obedience.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why facing one qibla is important for Muslims all over the world today.
parts.answer: It unites Muslims everywhere in one direction, from Indonesia to Canada, showing one community worshipping one God; it links them to Ibrahim and Isma'il who built the Ka'ba; it shows obedience to God's command; it gives a sense of belonging and discipline; it does not mean worshipping the Ka'ba, as Muslims worship only God.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed point up to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the prayers on the two Eids and the prayer at a funeral (janaza).
parts.answer: Eid prayers: offered in congregation in the morning of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, often in an open ground; two units with extra calls of 'God is Greatest'; no call to prayer is made; a sermon is given by the imam; Muslims wear their best clothes. Funeral prayer: a congregational prayer for a dead Muslim, offered standing with the body in front of the imam; there is no bowing or prostration; it includes praising God, blessings on the Prophet (pbuh) and prayers for forgiveness for the dead person; it is a communal duty.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for Eid prayer (time/place, two units with extra takbirs, no adhan, sermon) and up to 2 marks for funeral prayer (standing only, no bowing/prostration, prayers for the dead, communal duty).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A Muslim working night shifts in a hospital in Lahore finds it hard to keep all five prayers on time. Suggest how he can keep his prayers and explain why it is worth the effort.
parts.answer: He can learn the prayer times for his shift, use short breaks to pray in the hospital prayer room, ask his supervisor for a few minutes at prayer times, and set reminders; prayer brings calm and strength in stressful work and keeps him connected to God; showing commitment can also inspire colleagues.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed practical suggestion (max 2) and 1 mark per reason why it matters (max 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main rites of hajj from the 8th to the 10th of Dhu al-Hijja.
parts.answer: Pilgrims in ihram go to Mina on the 8th and pray there; on the 9th they go to the plain of 'Arafat and stand in prayer and supplication from midday to sunset (the most important rite); after sunset they go to Muzdalifa, pray and spend the night, and collect pebbles; on the 10th they throw seven pebbles at the large pillar (Jamrat al-'Aqaba) in Mina; they offer an animal sacrifice; men shave or shorten their hair and women cut a lock of hair; they return to Makka for the tawaf al-ifada around the Ka'ba (and the sa'i between Safa and Marwa if not done earlier).
parts.working: Indicative content: Mina on 8th; 'Arafat on 9th (standing / supplication); importance of 'Arafat; Muzdalifa night / pebbles; stoning Jamrat al-'Aqaba on 10th (seven pebbles); sacrifice; shaving/cutting hair; tawaf al-ifada; sa'i. parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe ihram and the restrictions it places on the pilgrim.
parts.answer: Ihram is the sacred state entered before reaching the miqat (boundary points) for hajj or 'umra, with the intention and the call of response to God (talbiya); men wear two plain, unstitched white sheets and women wear simple modest clothing with the face and hands uncovered; restrictions include: no cutting hair or nails, no perfume, no hunting, no cutting plants in the sacred area, no marriage contracts or marital relations, no quarrelling or bad language; men may not cover their heads.
