parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the simple clothing of ihram teaches pilgrims.
parts.answer: Everyone looks the same, so differences of wealth, nationality and status disappear; it reminds them of the burial shroud and the Day of Judgement; it encourages humility and focus on God rather than appearance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the rites of hajj recall the lives of the Prophet Ibrahim, his wife Hajar and their son Isma'il.
parts.answer: Ibrahim and Isma'il built the Ka'ba as a house for the worship of the One God (Sura 2.127), so tawaf around it recalls their work; Ibrahim called people to pilgrimage; the sa'i between Safa and Marwa recalls Hajar running between the two hills in search of water for her baby, and the spring of Zamzam that God made flow, from which pilgrims drink; the stoning of the pillars recalls Ibrahim's rejection of Satan's temptations; the sacrifice recalls Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son at God's command and God's ransoming him with a ram (Sura 37.102–107); the Station of Ibrahim near the Ka'ba marks where he stood.

parts.answer: e.g. combining trust in God with effort: she ran seven times searching, yet the water came from God; people today should work hard and trust God for the outcome (or: patience; the value of mothers' sacrifice).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the importance of the Day of 'Arafa for pilgrims.
parts.answer: On the 9th of Dhu al-Hijja pilgrims stand on the plain of 'Arafat from after midday until sunset; the Prophet (pbuh) taught that hajj is 'Arafa, so a pilgrim who misses it has missed the hajj; pilgrims spend the time in prayer, supplication and asking forgiveness; it was here that the Prophet (pbuh) gave his Farewell Sermon in 632 CE, and the verse saying the religion had been perfected was revealed; it reminds pilgrims of standing before God on the Day of Judgement (but is not to be confused with it).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: 9th Dhu al-Hijja; standing from midday to sunset; hajj is 'Arafa / essential rite; prayer and forgiveness; Farewell Sermon; completion of religion verse (5.3); reminder of the Day of Judgement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two teachings of the Farewell Sermon and explain their relevance today.
parts.answer: e.g. all people are equal, no Arab is better than a non-Arab, nor white than black, except by piety, which challenges racism today; the rights of women must be respected and husbands must treat wives kindly, relevant to family life; lives, property and honour are sacred, relevant to crime and corruption; interest was abolished, relevant to finance.
parts.working: For each of two teachings: 1 mark for the teaching, 1 mark for its modern relevance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sacrifice (qurbani) performed at Eid al-Adha and explain its meaning.
parts.answer: It is performed on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijja after the Eid prayer, and on the following days of Eid, by pilgrims and by Muslims around the world who can afford it; a healthy animal of the right age (sheep, goat, cow or camel) is slaughtered in God's name, humanely; a common recommended practice is to keep a third of the meat, give a third to relatives and friends and a third to the poor; it recalls Ibrahim's obedience; the Qur'an says it is not the meat or the blood that reaches God but the believers' piety (Sura 22.37).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: timing; who performs it; healthy animal / types; slaughter in God's name, humanely; sharing of meat (thirds); remembrance of Ibrahim; piety, not meat/blood, reaches God (22.37).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A family in Faisalabad sacrifices a goat that gives 18 kg of meat and divides it in three equal shares as recommended. How much meat goes to the poor?
parts.answer: 6 kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some Muslims living abroad pay a charity to carry out their sacrifice in a poor country. Do you think this keeps the meaning of the sacrifice? Give a reason.
parts.answer: Yes, mostly: the act of obedience and sharing with the needy is kept, and the meat reaches people who rarely eat it; but the family loses the personal experience and sharing with neighbours, so some do both.
parts.working: 1 mark: judgement with reason; 1 mark: counter-point or development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the stoning of the pillars (jamarat) during the days of hajj.
parts.answer: On the 10th of Dhu al-Hijja pilgrims throw seven small pebbles at the largest pillar, Jamrat al-'Aqaba; on the 11th and 12th (the days of tashriq) they throw seven pebbles at each of the three pillars, starting with the smallest; some stay for the 13th and stone the three pillars again; each throw is accompanied by saying 'God is Greatest'; the act recalls Ibrahim's rejection of Satan.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: 10th: seven at Jamrat al-'Aqaba; 11th and 12th: seven at each of three pillars; order (smallest first); optional 13th; takbir with each throw; symbolism (rejecting Satan).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of pebbles thrown by a pilgrim who leaves Mina on the 12th, and by one who stays for the 13th.
parts.answer: Leaves on the 12th: 7 + 21 + 21 = 49 pebbles. Stays for the 13th: 49 + 21 = 70 pebbles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the stoning teaches Muslims about resisting temptation in daily life.
parts.answer: It is a symbolic, repeated rejection of evil, reminding Muslims that temptation must be resisted again and again, e.g. refusing to cheat or to waste time on harmful content, and that God's help is sought in doing so.
parts.working: 1 mark: symbolism of rejecting evil repeatedly; 1 mark: modern application.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the lessons that hajj teaches about equality and unity of the Muslim community.
parts.answer: Millions of Muslims of every race, nation and language gather in one place at one time; all wear the same simple clothing, so rich and poor cannot be told apart; all perform the same rites in the same order, facing the same Ka'ba; they pray together and share hardships; the Farewell Sermon stresses that no one is superior except by piety; pilgrims return with a sense of a worldwide brotherhood.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The lessons of hajj are wasted if pilgrims return home and live as before.' How far do you agree? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Largely agree: hajj is meant to bring lasting change, and the Prophet (pbuh) said an accepted hajj returns a person sinless like a newborn, which brings the duty to start afresh; returning pilgrims should be more honest, patient and generous and less proud; however, even if a person slips, the forgiveness and experience still have value and can be renewed through repentance; a judgement with reasons is needed.
parts.working: Level marking. 1: simple view. 2: one reason explained. 3: two reasons or a counter-argument. 4: balanced, reasoned judgement with examples of change expected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the differences between hajj and 'umra.
parts.answer: Hajj is a pillar of Islam, obligatory once in a lifetime for those able; 'umra is not a pillar: most Hanafi and Maliki scholars regard it as a strongly recommended Sunna, while Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars hold it obligatory once in a lifetime; hajj can only be performed on fixed days in Dhu al-Hijja, while 'umra may be done at any time of year; hajj includes standing at 'Arafat, the nights at Muzdalifa and Mina, the stoning and the sacrifice; 'umra consists of ihram, tawaf, sa'i and shaving or cutting the hair, and takes only a few hours.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four contrasts: status (hajj a pillar; 'umra not a pillar — Sunna or once-obligatory depending on the school); timing (fixed vs any time); rites of hajj beyond 'umra; rites of 'umra; length.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Every year more Muslims apply for hajj than the number of places available, and governments use a quota system. Explain how Muslims should respond if they cannot go, and what alternatives Islam offers.
parts.answer: Hajj is only required for those who are able, and being unable because of the quota is a valid excuse; they should keep the sincere intention and try again; meanwhile they can fast on the Day of 'Arafa, offer a sacrifice at Eid al-Adha, perform 'umra if possible, and do extra good deeds in the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja, which are highly blessed; they should not use dishonest means (bribery or false documents) to obtain a place.
parts.working: 1 mark: not obligatory when unable / valid excuse; 1 mark: keep intention; 1 mark: alternatives (fasting 'Arafa, sacrifice, 'umra, good deeds in first ten days); 1 mark: rejection of dishonest means / developed point.

practice.subtopic: Festivals and days of special significance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr.
parts.answer: It is celebrated on the 1st of Shawwal, at the end of Ramadan, when the new moon is sighted; before the Eid prayer each household pays zakat al-fitr (a set amount of staple food or its value for each member) to the poor; Muslims bathe, wear new or best clothes and often eat something sweet before going to the prayer; they say 'God is Greatest' on the way; they attend the Eid prayer and sermon in congregation; they greet each other, visit relatives and friends, give gifts to children (eidi) and share food.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of zakat al-fitr.
parts.answer: It purifies the fasting person from any idle or bad talk during Ramadan; it ensures the poor can also celebrate Eid and have food on the day; it reminds the community that celebration must include everyone.

practice.subtopic: Festivals and days of special significance

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the celebration of Eid al-Adha.
parts.answer: It takes place on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijja, during the hajj; Muslims attend the Eid prayer in congregation in the morning; those who can afford it sacrifice an animal after the prayer, in memory of Ibrahim's obedience; the meat is shared with family, friends and the poor; people repeat 'God is Greatest' during the days of Eid; families visit one another and celebrate for several days.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: 10th Dhu al-Hijja; linked to hajj; Eid prayer; sacrifice after prayer; Ibrahim's obedience; sharing meat with poor; takbirs during the days of Eid; visits and celebration over several days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In some cities, waste from animal sacrifice creates hygiene problems. How can Muslims celebrate Eid al-Adha in a way that also respects the environment and their neighbours?
parts.answer: Sacrifice at approved slaughterhouses or designated places; dispose of waste properly and clean the area; avoid blocking streets or causing distress to neighbours; give some meat to non-Muslim neighbours; this follows Islamic teaching on cleanliness, not harming others and kindness to neighbours.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed practical point up to 3; 1 mark for linking to an Islamic teaching (cleanliness, no harm, rights of neighbours).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the Day of 'Ashura and the reasons it is significant for Muslims.
parts.answer: It is the 10th of Muharram; when the Prophet (pbuh) arrived in Madina he learned that the Jews fasted on this day to remember God saving the Prophet Musa and his people from Pharaoh; he fasted on it and encouraged Muslims to fast; later Ramadan became the obligatory fast and the 'Ashura fast remained voluntary; it is also the day on which Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet (pbuh), was martyred at Karbala in 680 CE, which Muslims, and especially Shi'a Muslims, remember with mourning and gatherings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: 10th Muharram; Musa saved from Pharaoh; Prophet (pbuh) fasted and encouraged it; became voluntary after Ramadan; martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala; remembrance/mourning gatherings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can Muslims remembering 'Ashura in Pakistan help to strengthen unity between different groups in the community?
parts.answer: By respecting each other's ways of remembering the day; joining in shared values such as standing against injustice, which Husayn's sacrifice represents, and gratitude for God's help to Musa; offering water and food to those in processions or gatherings; avoiding hurtful speech and co-operating with authorities for peace and security.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed point up to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the significance of the Day of 'Arafa for Muslims who are not on hajj, and of the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja.
parts.answer: The first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja are described as the best days of the year for good deeds; Muslims increase remembrance of God, saying 'God is Greatest', and do extra good works; those not on hajj are encouraged to fast on the Day of 'Arafa (9th), which the Prophet (pbuh) said expiates the sins of the previous year and the coming year; those planning to sacrifice often avoid cutting their hair and nails from the start of the month until the sacrifice.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: first ten days best for good deeds; extra remembrance/takbirs; fasting on 'Arafa for non-pilgrims; expiation of two years' sins; not cutting hair/nails before sacrifice; link with pilgrims' rites.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why do you think Muslims who are not on hajj are given ways to share in the blessings of these days?
parts.answer: Most Muslims cannot go on hajj, so God's mercy gives everyone an opportunity for reward and forgiveness; it links the worldwide community with the pilgrims in spirit; it keeps the meaning of Ibrahim's sacrifice alive at home; it shows that sincerity, not location, is what counts.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed reason up to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Islamic (Hijri) calendar was established and how it works.
parts.answer: It was introduced during the caliphate of 'Umar, who, after consulting the Companions, chose the year of the migration (622 CE) as its starting point; it is a lunar calendar of twelve months, each beginning with the sighting of the new moon; the year begins with Muharram; months include Ramadan (fasting), Shawwal (Eid al-Fitr) and Dhu al-Hijja (hajj and Eid al-Adha); a lunar year is about 354 days.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: introduced by 'Umar; consultation; starts from hijra 622 CE; lunar; twelve months; moon sighting; first month Muharram; about 354 days; festivals linked to months.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: About 11 days.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one benefit for Muslims of festivals and fasting moving through all the seasons over the years.
parts.answer: Over about 33 years Muslims in every country fast in both long summer days and short winter days, so no region is always favoured or burdened; this is fair to Muslims worldwide and teaches adaptability and patience.
parts.working: 1 mark: moves through seasons; 1 mark: fairness for all regions; 1 mark: developed lesson.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the Islamic festivals combine worship with celebration.
parts.answer: Both Eids begin with congregational prayer and sermon; they follow acts of worship (the fast of Ramadan; the hajj); they include remembrance of God through takbirs; charity is built in (zakat al-fitr, sharing sacrifice meat); then families and communities celebrate with food, new clothes, visits and gifts; enjoyment is lawful but within Islamic limits.

parts.answer: Partly agree: spending on clothes, food and gifts can overshadow prayer and charity, and debt or waste can result; but most Muslims still attend the Eid prayer, pay zakat al-fitr and visit relatives, and celebrating God's blessings is itself encouraged; the balance depends on individuals and families keeping worship and charity central.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the meaning of jihad and describe its different forms.
parts.answer: Jihad means striving or struggling in the way of God; the greater jihad is the struggle against one's own selfish desires and temptations to become a better Muslim; jihad of the tongue/pen is speaking and writing for truth and justice, including speaking a just word before an unjust ruler; jihad through wealth is spending for good causes; jihad of the hand includes working to change wrong by action, such as serving the community; the lesser, armed jihad is fighting in defence of Muslims or against oppression, under strict conditions and rightful authority.

parts.answer: A Muslim could explain calmly that the Prophet (pbuh) did not control when or how revelation came, that its arrival was a heavy physical experience, and that he himself distinguished it from his own words (his Hadith), so Muslims believe it is the word of God; the reply should be respectful and invite further discussion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pause in revelation (fatra) after the first revelation, and the revelation that ended it.
parts.answer: After the first revelation there was a period when no more verses came; the Prophet (pbuh) was deeply worried and distressed, unsure whether he would receive revelation again; then he saw the angel again between the sky and the earth and was frightened, went home and asked to be wrapped; the opening verses of Sura 74 (al-Muddaththir) were revealed, telling the one wrapped in a cloak to arise and warn, glorify his Lord, keep clean and avoid idols; after this revelation came regularly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: revelation stopped for a time; Prophet (pbuh) anxious/sad; saw the angel again (between sky and earth); returned home and asked to be covered; Sura 74 revealed; command to arise and warn; glorify the Lord / purify clothes / avoid idols; revelation continued regularly afterwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The pause in revelation shows that the Prophet (pbuh) could not produce the Qur'an himself.' To what extent do you agree? Give reasons.
parts.answer: Agree largely: if he were the author he could have continued at will, yet he waited anxiously and was distressed; the timing of revelation was outside his control, which supports Muslim belief that it came from God. A balanced answer may add that the pause also prepared him for the mission and that belief rests on many other signs too (its content, his honesty), so it is one strong piece of evidence among others.
parts.working: Level marking. 1 mark: simple agree/disagree. 2 marks: one reason explained (he could not control timing; his distress). 3–4 marks: developed reasoning with a judgement, e.g. recognises the pause as supporting evidence alongside other reasons (his truthfulness, the Qur'an's content).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Prophet's opponents in Makka reacted to the revelations, and how the Qur'an responded to their claims.
parts.answer: They rejected the message and mocked it; they called the Prophet (pbuh) a poet, a soothsayer (kahin), a madman or a sorcerer; they said the verses were only 'tales of the ancients' or that a foreign man was teaching him; they demanded miracles instead; the Qur'an denied each claim (e.g. it is not the word of a poet or a soothsayer, Sura 69.41–42; the man they point to speaks a foreign tongue while the Qur'an is in clear Arabic, Sura 16.103); it challenged them to produce a book like it, then ten suras, then even one sura like it (e.g. Sura 2.23, 11.13), and they could not.
parts.working: Indicative content: Rejection/mockery; called him poet; soothsayer; madman/sorcerer; 'tales of the ancients' / taught by a foreigner; demanded miracles; Qur'an denied the claims (example); challenge to produce something like it; challenge reduced to ten suras / one sura; they failed to meet it. parts.answer: The Makkans were masters of Arabic poetry and eloquence and were desperate to defeat the message, yet none could produce even one sura like it; the Prophet (pbuh) was not known as a poet and could not read or write; so Muslims see its unmatched language and content (its inimitability) as a sign that it is God's word, not human composition.

parts.text: Write about the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) and its link with the revelation of the Qur'an.
parts.answer: It is the night in Ramadan on which the Qur'an began to be revealed; Sura 97 says it is better than a thousand months and that angels and the Spirit descend by God's permission, and that it is peace until dawn; its exact date is not fixed, and Muslims seek it in the odd nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan; many spend these nights in prayer, recitation and i'tikaf.

parts.text: Why do you think the exact date of the Night of Power is not known? Explain how this affects the way Muslims worship.
parts.answer: Because it is hidden, Muslims make extra effort across several nights rather than one, which increases worship, sincerity and self-discipline; it keeps believers hopeful and humble; communities in mosques from Lahore to London fill the last ten nights with prayer, so the whole end of Ramadan becomes a time of spiritual effort.

parts.text: Describe how the Qur'an was preserved during the lifetime of the Prophet (pbuh).
parts.answer: Revelations were memorised by the Prophet (pbuh) and by many Companions (huffaz) and recited in daily prayers; they were written down by scribes such as Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Ali and Ubayy ibn Ka'b on materials such as palm leaves, flat stones, animal bones, leather and parchment; the Prophet (pbuh) told the scribes the position of each verse; he checked what was written; Jibril reviewed the revelation with him each Ramadan, twice in the last year; but it was not yet gathered into one volume because revelation was still continuing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Qur'an and the Sunna of the Prophet (pbuh) work together as sources of law, using the example of prayer.
parts.answer: The Qur'an commands prayer, mentions its times broadly, purification, bowing and prostration, and the Friday prayer; it does not give the number of units or exact actions; the Prophet (pbuh) explained and showed them, telling the Companions to pray in the way they had seen him pray; so the Sunna explains, details and applies the Qur'an's commands; the Qur'an itself orders obedience to the Prophet (pbuh); the Sunna never contradicts the Qur'an.

parts.text: Describe the conversation between the Prophet (pbuh) and Mu'adh ibn Jabal when the Prophet sent him as a judge to Yemen, and explain what it shows about the order of the sources of law.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Qur'an forbade alcohol in stages. Describe these stages.
parts.answer: First, it said wine and gambling contain some benefit but their sin is greater (Sura 2.219); next, believers were told not to come to prayer while intoxicated (Sura 4.43); finally, intoxicants and gambling were declared a filthy work of Satan to be avoided completely (Sura 5.90–91); the Companions poured away their wine so that it ran in the streets of Madina.
parts.working: 1 mark per stage (3 stages) and 1 mark for the Companions' response or for correct references. Maximum 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What principle of law-making does this show, and how could it guide a government in a Muslim country today?
parts.answer: It shows gradualness and wisdom: people were prepared step by step, with reasons given, before a full ban; a government could introduce reforms (e.g. reducing smoking or drug use, ending interest in banking) in stages with education and support so that people accept and keep them.
parts.working: 1 mark: principle (gradual / with reasons); 1 mark: explanation of why it works; 1–2 marks: modern application with example.

practice.subtopic: The Qur'an as a source of Islamic law

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Muslim jurists use the Qur'an when a modern practice is not mentioned in it by name, such as a new online betting game.
parts.answer: They search the Qur'an and Sunna for related rulings: the Qur'an forbids gambling (maysir) together with intoxicants as the work of Satan (Sura 5.90–91); they identify what makes maysir forbidden (gaining money by pure chance at another's loss, which causes enmity and distracts from God); they check whether the new game has the same features — if it does, the same ruling applies whatever its form (qiyas); they also consider general Qur'anic principles such as not consuming others' wealth unjustly (Sura 4.29) and avoiding harm and waste; they look for agreement among scholars (ijma').
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: look first for direct text (5.90–91 on gambling); identify the cause/features of the original ruling; apply the ruling to the new case with the same features (analogy); general principles (no unjust taking of wealth, avoid harm/waste); consensus of scholars.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Why is it important that such rulings are made by qualified scholars rather than by individuals for themselves?
parts.answer: Scholars know Arabic, the Qur'an and Sunna, earlier rulings and the methods of reasoning; this prevents mistakes and rulings based on personal desire; agreed rulings keep the community united; individuals may still study and ask questions, but final rulings need expertise, as in medicine or engineering.
parts.working: 1 mark per developed reason, up to 4: expertise/knowledge; avoid error/desire; unity of community; analogy with other expert fields.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the meaning of qiyas (analogy) and how it is based on the Qur'an. Give an example.
parts.answer: Qiyas is applying a ruling from the Qur'an or Sunna to a new case that has the same underlying reason (cause, 'illa); it is used only when the Qur'an and Sunna have no direct ruling and there is no consensus; example: the Qur'an forbids wine (khamr) because it intoxicates and leads people away from remembering God (Sura 5.90–91), so scholars apply the same ruling to other intoxicants such as harmful drugs; another example: the Qur'an tells believers to leave trade at the call to Friday prayer (Sura 62.9), so other activities that distract from it are also not allowed at that time.
parts.working: Indicative content: Definition — analogy, applying an existing ruling to a new case; the shared cause ('illa); used only when there is no direct text or consensus; based on the Qur'an's call to reflect and reason, and on the Prophet's approval of Mu'adh; accurate example showing the original ruling, the reason and the new case (e.g. wine forbidden because it intoxicates, so drugs are forbidden). parts.label: a
parts.text: Give examples of concessions (rulings that make things easier in hardship) found in the Qur'an.
parts.answer: A sick person or traveller may miss fasts in Ramadan and make them up later, and those who cannot fast may feed a poor person instead (Sura 2.184–185); travellers may shorten prayers when on a journey (Sura 4.101); when water is not available or would cause harm, tayammum with clean earth replaces washing (Sura 4.43, 5.6); a person forced by necessity may eat otherwise forbidden food to stay alive (Sura 2.173); hajj is required only of those who are able (Sura 3.97); a person forced to deny faith under threat is excused while the heart remains firm (Sura 16.106).

parts.text: Describe what is meant by shirk and give examples of its different forms.
parts.answer: Shirk is associating partners with God, the opposite of tawhid. Forms include worshipping idols or created things such as the sun or moon; believing God has a son, wife or partners; giving God's unique attributes, such as complete knowledge of the unseen or power to create, to others; and hidden or minor shirk, such as doing good deeds to show off rather than for God.

parts.answer: The trumpet will be blown and the universe will end; all people will be raised from their graves and gathered before God; each person's record of deeds will be given — in the right hand to the successful and in the left hand to the losers; deeds will be weighed on the scales; witnesses will speak, including people's own limbs and the earth itself; people will cross the bridge over Hell; God will judge with perfect justice and mercy; the Prophet (pbuh) will intercede by God's permission.
parts.working: Indicative content: Trumpet / destruction of the universe; resurrection; gathering before God; book of deeds in right or left hand; scales; even an atom's weight counted (Sura 99); limbs and earth bear witness; bridge (sirat); intercession by God's permission; justice — no one wronged; mercy; final destination. parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Qur'an presents Paradise and Hell.
parts.answer: Paradise: eternal gardens with rivers flowing beneath, peace and no sorrow, fruits and pleasures, being with loved ones, and above all God's pleasure; it is the reward for faith and good deeds. Hell: a place of fire and severe punishment, regret and despair, for those who rejected God and did great evil; both are described vividly to encourage good and warn against evil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why belief in life after death is important for Muslims.
parts.answer: It gives meaning and purpose to life as a test; it guarantees final justice, since many wrongs are not punished in this world; it motivates good deeds and discourages sin; it gives comfort in suffering and loss, as the believer hopes to meet loved ones; it reminds people that wealth and status are temporary; without it, belief in God's justice would be incomplete.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what Muslims believe about barzakh and the questioning in the grave.
parts.answer: Barzakh is the barrier or stage between death and the resurrection; after burial two angels, known in tradition as Munkar and Nakir, question the dead person about who their Lord is, what their religion is and who their prophet was; believers answer correctly and their grave becomes spacious and peaceful; those who rejected faith cannot answer and suffer; the soul remains in this state until the Day of Resurrection.
parts.working: Indicative content: Barzakh means barrier / interval; between death and resurrection; questioning by two angels (Munkar and Nakir); questions about Lord, religion and prophet; believers answer and are at peace; disbelievers fail and suffer; foretaste of the final outcome; no return to the world for a second chance. parts.text: Describe what Muslims believe about the nature of angels.
parts.answer: Angels are created by God from light; they are unseen beings, without free will, who always obey God; they do not eat, drink, marry or tire; they worship and praise God constantly; they can take different forms, including human form, by God's permission; they have different duties; belief in them is an Article of Faith.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name four angels and describe the duties of each.
parts.answer: Jibril (Gabriel) brings revelation to the prophets; Mika'il (Michael) is responsible for rain and provision; Israfil will blow the trumpet at the end of the world and for the resurrection; the Angel of Death (often called 'Izra'il) takes souls; the noble recording angels (Kiraman Katibin) write each person's deeds; Munkar and Nakir question the dead in the grave; Malik guards Hell; Ridwan guards Paradise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write about the role of the angel Jibril in the life of the Prophet (pbuh).
parts.answer: Jibril brought the first revelation in the cave of Hira and continued to bring the Qur'an over about twenty-three years; he accompanied the Prophet (pbuh) on the Night Journey and Ascension; he taught him how to perform the prayers; he came in human form to ask about Islam, faith and excellence, teaching the Companions; he reviewed the Qur'an with the Prophet (pbuh) every Ramadan, twice in the final year; he supported him at difficult times, such as at Ta'if with the angel of the mountains.

parts.text: Explain the differences between angels, jinn and human beings in Islamic belief.
parts.answer: Angels are made from light, have no free will and always obey God; jinn are made from smokeless fire, are unseen, have free will and can be believers or disbelievers — Iblis was one of the jinn; humans are made from clay, have free will and are given the role of vicegerent; jinn and humans will be judged on their choices, while angels are not tested in the same way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what Muslims mean by belief in al-qadr (divine decree).
parts.answer: God knows everything that has happened and will happen; everything is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz); nothing happens except by God's will; God is the Creator of everything, including human actions; yet humans have been given free will to choose and are responsible for their choices; belief in decree, good and bad, is an Article of Faith.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'If God has decreed everything, humans cannot be responsible for what they do.' Explain how Muslims answer this argument.
parts.answer: God's knowledge of what people will choose does not force them to choose it; humans are given intellect, guidance and free will, and they experience making real choices; God's justice requires accountability only for what people chose; people are not held responsible for what is outside their control; therefore decree and responsibility exist together, and the decree cannot be used as an excuse for sin.
